cim_eredeti: Atlassian AI chief says PMs must steer, not code
szoveg_eredeti:
Sherif Mansour, head of AI and product craft at Atlassian, told Lenny's Podcast that the job of product manager did not disappear when AI coding arrived, it narrowed to direction. Mansour, who has spent 17 years at Atlassian according to The Futurist account of the conversation, said an early experiment that turned PMs and designers into full-time AI builders fell apart after a month.

Throughput was not the problem. Direction was.

That failed experiment is why Mansour argues PMs own decision making velocity, not decisions themselves. The best PMs build a shared brain, meaning a common understanding of customer, product and business context that lets engineers and designers act without waiting for a spec. He names three contexts to fill, customer context, product and market context, and the business you operate in, and said trust breaks once a group grows past 20 or 30 people unless someone maintains that shared base.

So the workflow change is concrete. Mansour said he tries never to do a customer interview without engineers in the room, and he cited PMs who send every engineer to test AI tools and report back, plus engineers staffing booths with him at customer events. He pointed to a 2010 Confluence interview where customers used red and green stars to mark unfinished work, and said an engineer in the room proposed the checkbox in the page, an idea he said did not exist on the web at the time.

Hiring is where he gets prescriptive. Mansour uses a triangle credited to Geoff Redfern, with general manager, scientist and artist as the three corners that describe how a PM naturally does discovery, from TAM and revenue math to hypothesis testing to vision-led taste. He said few people do all three well, so leaders should stop throwing PM bodies at a problem and match the archetype to the work, with all-rounders reserved for zero-to-one teams. He admitted the model is aimed at medium to large organizations, not startups, and he joked that he is a strong artist and a terrible general manager.

That also frames his answer on juniors. Mansour said on Lenny's Podcast that the idea you no longer need to hire juniors is a misconception, in part because they bring new working norms. His example was his 12-year-old son, who he said went straight to vibe coding games without learning syntax and treats that as normal. Watch for teams that hire for a spike, state the weakness plainly, and pair opposites, as Mansour said he does with his colleague Jamille, rather than asking every PM to ship code.
